content.content:
# arg3-longterm-tests

The ARG3 move-up longterm test as three NOVA apps that do the same thing
through three different stacks, so the overhead of each can be compared, plus
three more apps that reproduce specific problems on the same foundation:

| directory | app | talks to NOVA via | run model |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `sdk/` | `audi-arg3-sdk` | NOVA Python SDK + NOVAx | one `run_program.py` process per robot |
| `api/` | `audi-arg3-api` | generated Python API client only | one `run_robot.py` process per robot |
| `rust/` | `audi-arg3-rust` | Rust client (vendored) | one tokio task per robot |
| `tcpswitch/` | `audi-arg3-tcpswitch` | NOVA Python SDK + NOVAx (same pin as `sdk/`) | one `run_program.py` process per robot |
| `pause/` | `audi-arg3-pause` | NOVA Python SDK + NOVAx (its **own** pin, see below) | one `run_program.py` process per robot |
| `pause-api/` | `audi-arg3-pause-api` | generated Python API client only | one `run_robot.py` process per robot |

The first three: same motions, same IO gating (`start` as run-enable, `stop`
to end the loop), same plan-once/execute-many loop, same operator UI.

`tcpswitch/` keeps the gating, the run model and the UI, but each cycle rotates
joint 0 by a preset angle and back, **planned and executed with the next TCP of
an operator-chosen sequence** — the repro for controller disconnects seen when
two successive executions change TCP.

`pause/` rotates joint 0 the same way, but **moves the gating inside the
execution**: every cycle commands `execute()` straight away with `pause_on_io`
armed on the enable signal, so the controller decides whether the robot moves.
It reproduces a robot that stays in standstill at the start of an execution
although the signal allows motion. Two consequences worth knowing before
reading its code: its "wait IO" is the enable signal rather than a pre-motion
gate, and it pins the SDK's interlock branch instead of sharing `sdk/`'s pin,
because `pause_on_io` exists nowhere else.

`pause-api/` is `pause/` without the SDK, the way `api/` is `sdk/` without it:
same cycles, options, scenarios, observer and UI, with the SDK's pause/resume
machinery rebuilt on the API client from what it is for (arm the condition on
every start, read pause/resume/end from the state stream, resume when the
signal clears, pause from the client when the bus goes away). It exists to
answer whether the stall `pause/` reproduces is the SDK's. Its `CLAUDE.md` maps
each SDK piece to its counterpart and lists the deliberate differences.

Each app's own `CLAUDE.md` and `README.md` carry its rules and findings;
`api/CLAUDE.md` holds the API protocol knowledge the others build on.

## The shared operator UI

`ui/` is the one frontend all six apps serve; `<app>/static/` are
byte-identical copies (every app is built from its own directory, and rust
embeds them with `include_str!`, so a UI change needs a rust rebuild). Edit
`ui/`, then:

```bash
scripts/sync-ui.sh          # copy into rust/, api/, sdk/, tcpswitch/, pause/, pause-api/ static
scripts/sync-ui.sh --check  # fail if any copy drifted
```

The frontend has no variant-specific code. Everything that differs comes from
each backend's `GET /api/config`: `title`, `variant` (label and accent-colour
key — rust orange, api teal, sdk violet, tcpswitch amber, pause magenta,
pause-api blue),
`run_options` (extra per-run switches a variant offers: rust, api, sdk, pause
and pause-api have `state_rate_ms`, sdk, pause and pause-api add `verbose`,
tcpswitch, pause and pause-api have `degrees` and `direction`, pause and
pause-api add `scenario`, `enable_delay_ms`, `fail_after_stall_s`, `stall_s`,
`gap_ms` and `replan`, and pause-api alone `restart_after_ms`) and
`tcp_selection` (`"single"`, the
default, renders one TCP dropdown per robot; `"sequence"` renders an ordered
multi-select and sends `tcps: [...]` per robot), and `log_view` (see below).
The backends serve the same JSON contract — controllers with TCPs (tcpswitch
adds `tcp_labels`), IO read/toggle/create/delete + SSE,
`/api/run`/`/api/stop`/`/api/status/stream`, file-based `/api/logs`,
`/api/health`.

## Reading a log

A log file is `LOG_MAX_BYTES` (10 MB by default), so the viewer never loads one
whole. Three endpoints, the same in all six apps:

| endpoint | what it does |
| --- | --- |
| `GET /api/logs/file/{name}` | downloads the file, as before |
| `GET /api/logs/view/{name}?offset&limit` | one byte window as JSON; no `offset` means the tail |
| `GET /api/logs/stream/{name}?offset` | SSE: `append`, `gap`, `rotated`, `gone` |

`/api/config` advertises support as `"log_view": {"follow": true}`; a backend
that omits the key gets the old download-only Logs panel, so the apps can
gain this at different times without the UI growing a button that 404s.

Two things worth knowing before touching it:

- **`text` is a lossy UTF-8 decode of the bytes `[start, end)`, so its
  character length is not `end - start`.** Page and follow from `end`, never
  from `text.length`.
- **The follower re-stats the path, it does not hold a descriptor.** Both
  writers rotate by rename+recreate, so a held descriptor would go on reading
  the renamed `.log.1` and never notice.

`tests/log-window-cases.json` is the contract the six implementations share.
rust checks itself against it in `cargo test`; the Python apps have no test
suite, so `scripts/check-log-contract.py` runs the same cases by hand:

```bash
cd api && uv run ../scripts/check-log-contract.py audi_arg3_api
cd sdk && uv run ../scripts/check-log-contract.py audi_arg3
cd tcpswitch && uv run ../scripts/check-log-contract.py audi_arg3_tcpswitch
cd pause && uv run ../scripts/check-log-contract.py audi_arg3_pause
cd pause-api && uv run ../scripts/check-log-contract.py audi_arg3_pause_api
```

`run_options` are rendered generically as `select`, `bool` or `number` inputs
and posted back as `options` on `POST /api/run`; every value except a checkbox
arrives at the backend as a **string**, so each backend coerces.

## The state-stream rate is the same knob in every variant

`state_rate_ms` is a per-run option in the three move-up apps and in `pause/`
and `pause-api/` (env `STATE_RESPONSE_RATE_MS` sets the default, which differs:
rust 0, api 200, sdk 0, pause 0, pause-api 0). **0 means the controller's own step rate, and they request it
the same way — by not sending a rate at all**: the Python API client omits
`response_rate`, the SDK passes `state_stream_rate_msecs=None`, rust passes
`None` rather than the `cycle_time` it resolved for the log line. A rate
comparison then compares only the client, not the request.

In `pause/` this knob feeds the stream the SDK's execution state machine reads
to decide that a pause happened and that a resume happened, so it is a variable
under test there rather than only an overhead measurement. That app's observer
therefore streams on its own socket at its own rate (`OBSERVE_STATE_RATE_MS`).
`pause-api/` reads the same knob for its own pause/resume/end detection, on a
websocket of its own per execution rather than the SDK's shared one.

## The SDK pins are not all the same

`sdk/` and `tcpswitch/` share one commit on purpose, so the TCP-switch repro
differs from the move-up app in nothing but the motion. `pause/` does not: it
tracks `lab/interlock-with-pause`, because `pause_on_io` and its resume
machinery exist only there. Every `pause/` run logs the installed
`wandelbots-nova` version on its first lines, so a log always says which SDK
produced it.

## Rules that hold for all six

- **Never hardcode an instance address.** `GET {basePath}/api/health` says
  what an app is actually talking to.
- **Confirm virtual vs physical before anything with physical consequences.**
- **The UI must not put work on the robots' path.** Push (SSE from NATS),
  don't poll; nothing per state frame or per log line *on the writer's side*.
  Logs stay on disk and are read from it, in bounded windows, only while an
  operator is looking — see "Reading a log" below.
- **No retries around motions.** A failed robot stays failed until the
  operator restarts it.

# arg3-longterm-tests

The ARG3 move-up longterm test as three NOVA apps that do the same thing
through three different stacks, so the overhead of each can be compared, plus
three more apps that reproduce specific problems on the same foundation:

| directory | app | talks to NOVA via | run model |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `sdk/` | `audi-arg3-sdk` | NOVA Python SDK + NOVAx | one `run_program.py` process per robot |
| `api/` | `audi-arg3-api` | generated Python API client only | one `run_robot.py` process per robot |
| `rust/` | `audi-arg3-rust` | Rust client (vendored) | one tokio task per robot |
| `tcpswitch/` | `audi-arg3-tcpswitch` | NOVA Python SDK + NOVAx (same pin as `sdk/`) | one `run_program.py` process per robot |
| `pause/` | `audi-arg3-pause` | NOVA Python SDK + NOVAx (its **own** pin, see below) | one `run_program.py` process per robot |
| `pause-api/` | `audi-arg3-pause-api` | generated Python API client only | one `run_robot.py` process per robot |

The first three: same motions, same IO gating (`start` as run-enable, `stop`
to end the loop), same plan-once/execute-many loop, same operator UI.

`tcpswitch/` keeps the gating, the run model and the UI, but each cycle rotates
joint 0 by a preset angle and back, **planned and executed with the next TCP of
an operator-chosen sequence** — the repro for controller disconnects seen when
two successive executions change TCP.

`pause/` rotates joint 0 the same way, but **moves the gating inside the
execution**: every cycle commands `execute()` straight away with `pause_on_io`
armed on the enable signal, so the controller decides whether the robot moves.
It reproduces a robot that stays in standstill at the start of an execution
although the signal allows motion. Two consequences worth knowing before
reading its code: its "wait IO" is the enable signal rather than a pre-motion
gate, and it pins the SDK's interlock branch instead of sharing `sdk/`'s pin,
because `pause_on_io` exists nowhere else.

`pause-api/` is `pause/` without the SDK, the way `api/` is `sdk/` without it:
same cycles, options, scenarios, observer and UI, with the SDK's pause/resume
machinery rebuilt on the API client from what it is for (arm the condition on
every start, read pause/resume/end from the state stream, resume when the
signal clears, pause from the client when the bus goes away). It exists to
answer whether the stall `pause/` reproduces is the SDK's. Its `CLAUDE.md` maps
each SDK piece to its counterpart and lists the deliberate differences.

Each app's own `CLAUDE.md` and `README.md` carry its rules and findings;
`api/CLAUDE.md` holds the API protocol knowledge the others build on.

## The shared operator UI

`ui/` is the one frontend all six apps serve; `<app>/static/` are
byte-identical copies (every app is built from its own directory, and rust
embeds them with `include_str!`, so a UI change needs a rust rebuild). Edit
`ui/`, then:

```bash
scripts/sync-ui.sh          # copy into rust/, api/, sdk/, tcpswitch/, pause/, pause-api/ static
scripts/sync-ui.sh --check  # fail if any copy drifted
```

The frontend has no variant-specific code. Everything that differs comes from
each backend's `GET /api/config`: `title`, `variant` (label and accent-colour
key — rust orange, api teal, sdk violet, tcpswitch amber, pause magenta,
pause-api blue),
`run_options` (extra per-run switches a variant offers: rust, api, sdk, pause
and pause-api have `state_rate_ms`, sdk, pause and pause-api add `verbose`,
tcpswitch, pause and pause-api have `degrees` and `direction`, pause and
pause-api add `scenario`, `enable_delay_ms`, `fail_after_stall_s`, `stall_s`,
`gap_ms` and `replan`, and pause-api alone `restart_after_ms`) and
`tcp_selection` (`"single"`, the
default, renders one TCP dropdown per robot; `"sequence"` renders an ordered
multi-select and sends `tcps: [...]` per robot), and `log_view` (see below).
The backends serve the same JSON contract — controllers with TCPs (tcpswitch
adds `tcp_labels`), IO read/toggle/create/delete + SSE,
`/api/run`/`/api/stop`/`/api/status/stream`, file-based `/api/logs`,
`/api/health`.

## Reading a log

A log file is `LOG_MAX_BYTES` (10 MB by default), so the viewer never loads one
whole. Three endpoints, the same in all six apps:

| endpoint | what it does |
| --- | --- |
| `GET /api/logs/file/{name}` | downloads the file, as before |
| `GET /api/logs/view/{name}?offset&limit` | one byte window as JSON; no `offset` means the tail |
| `GET /api/logs/stream/{name}?offset` | SSE: `append`, `gap`, `rotated`, `gone` |

`/api/config` advertises support as `"log_view": {"follow": true}`; a backend
that omits the key gets the old download-only Logs panel, so the apps can
gain this at different times without the UI growing a button that 404s.

Two things worth knowing before touching it:

- **`text` is a lossy UTF-8 decode of the bytes `[start, end)`, so its
  character length is not `end - start`.** Page and follow from `end`, never
  from `text.length`.
- **The follower re-stats the path, it does not hold a descriptor.** Both
  writers rotate by rename+recreate, so a held descriptor would go on reading
  the renamed `.log.1` and never notice.

`tests/log-window-cases.json` is the contract the six implementations share.
rust checks itself against it in `cargo test`; the Python apps have no test
suite, so `scripts/check-log-contract.py` runs the same cases by hand:

```bash
cd api && uv run ../scripts/check-log-contract.py audi_arg3_api
cd sdk && uv run ../scripts/check-log-contract.py audi_arg3
cd tcpswitch && uv run ../scripts/check-log-contract.py audi_arg3_tcpswitch
cd pause && uv run ../scripts/check-log-contract.py audi_arg3_pause
cd pause-api && uv run ../scripts/check-log-contract.py audi_arg3_pause_api
```

`run_options` are rendered generically as `select`, `bool` or `number` inputs
and posted back as `options` on `POST /api/run`; every value except a checkbox
arrives at the backend as a **string**, so each backend coerces.

## The state-stream rate is the same knob in every variant

`state_rate_ms` is a per-run option in the three move-up apps and in `pause/`
and `pause-api/` (env `STATE_RESPONSE_RATE_MS` sets the default, which differs:
rust 0, api 200, sdk 0, pause 0, pause-api 0). **0 means the controller's own step rate, and they request it
the same way — by not sending a rate at all**: the Python API client omits
`response_rate`, the SDK passes `state_stream_rate_msecs=None`, rust passes
`None` rather than the `cycle_time` it resolved for the log line. A rate
comparison then compares only the client, not the request.

In `pause/` this knob feeds the stream the SDK's execution state machine reads
to decide that a pause happened and that a resume happened, so it is a variable
under test there rather than only an overhead measurement. That app's observer
therefore streams on its own socket at its own rate (`OBSERVE_STATE_RATE_MS`).
`pause-api/` reads the same knob for its own pause/resume/end detection, on a
websocket of its own per execution rather than the SDK's shared one.

## The SDK pins are not all the same

`sdk/` and `tcpswitch/` share one commit on purpose, so the TCP-switch repro
differs from the move-up app in nothing but the motion. `pause/` does not: it
tracks `lab/interlock-with-pause`, because `pause_on_io` and its resume
machinery exist only there. Every `pause/` run logs the installed
`wandelbots-nova` version on its first lines, so a log always says which SDK
produced it.

## Rules that hold for all six

- **Never hardcode an instance address.** `GET {basePath}/api/health` says
  what an app is actually talking to.
- **Confirm virtual vs physical before anything with physical consequences.**
- **The UI must not put work on the robots' path.** Push (SSE from NATS),
  don't poll; nothing per state frame or per log line *on the writer's side*.
  Logs stay on disk and are read from it, in bounded windows, only while an
  operator is looking — see "Reading a log" below.
- **No retries around motions.** A failed robot stays failed until the
  operator restarts it.

# CLAUDE.md

This file provides guidance to Claude Code (claude.ai/code) when working with code in this repository.

## What this is

A Wandelbots **NOVA app** (FastAPI via NOVAx, built on the NOVA Python SDK) that reproduces a
**robot that stays in standstill at the start of an execution although its enable signal allows
motion**. It deploys as **`audi-arg3-pause`**; the python package is `audi_arg3_pause`.

It is the fifth app in this repo and a close sibling of `../sdk` and `../tcpswitch` (same run
model, same operator UI, same two bus IOs). Three things differ, and all three are the point:

- **The gating happens inside the execution, not before it.** The other apps `wait_for_bus_io`
  on `start` and only then `execute()`. Here every cycle commands `execute()` immediately with
  `pause_on_io` armed on the enable signal and lets the *controller* decide whether the robot
  moves. Do not add a pre-motion wait: it would hide exactly what is being reproduced.
- **`wait_io` means the enable signal.** The shared UI's "wait IO" field is reused for it
  (default `start`), because it already carries an IO name with bus-IO suggestions and the
  create/delete buttons. `stop` ends the loop as everywhere else.
- **The enable signal can be driven by the app**, under `scenario`
  (`manual` / `enabled_once` / `auto_resume`). Only `auto_resume` writes it, and the default is
  `manual` because on a real cell that signal is PLC-facing and shared with the sibling apps.
  `enabled_once` deliberately runs **one execution per process**: the question is whether the
  *first* execution moves, so a fresh cursor, machine and websocket per trial is the point --
  do not "optimise" it into a loop.
- **`observe.py` is half the app.** The claim under test is "the signal says move and the robot
  does not", and neither half of that can be read from the SDK, since `execute()` is the
  suspect. Two independent watchers supply the evidence.

The SDK pin is **not** shared with `../sdk`: `pause_on_io` only exists on the interlock branch
(`lab/interlock-with-pause`, currently `e73ece8b`). Every run logs the installed
`wandelbots-nova` version on its first lines, so a log always says which SDK produced it.

Everything else -- one `run_program.py` process per robot, per-robot rotating log files, status
from the SDK's own NATS events, the shared UI -- is the `../sdk` design. Read `../sdk/CLAUDE.md`
for the deployment gotchas (Skaffold `resourceSelector`, `DEV_RELOAD` + `INSTALL_DEV`, never set
`NOVA_API`/`BASE_PATH` in `k8s/app.yaml`, the Dockerfile must copy `uv.lock`); they all apply
unchanged.

There is no pytest suite. `scripts/check_stall_detector.py` is the one thing that is checked
automatically, and it needs no instance.

**Branch `pause-auto-resume`** pins the SDK to `lab/pause-auto-resume` and adds the run options
`resume` (`sdk`|`controller`) and `missed_auto_resume` (`fail`|`start`).
`programs._apply_resume_strategy` sets the SDK's process-wide `ExecutionPolicy` from them at the
start of every run (one `run_program.py` process per robot keeps it per robot). See README,
"Resume strategy".

## Commands

```bash
uv sync --locked                                   # create venv + install deps
uv run python -m audi_arg3_pause                   # run the app on :3000 (blocks)
uv run python -m audi_arg3_pause.run_program <controller> --tcp 1 --wait-io start --stall-s 10
uv run python scripts/check_stall_detector.py      # offline: the stall/linger classification
uv run ruff format && uv run ruff check --select I --fix
skaffold dev --cleanup=false --status-check=false  # in-cluster dev, see ../sdk/CLAUDE.md
```

Endpoints: `/ui` (operator UI), `/api/*` (its backing API), `/programs` (NOVAx), `/api/health`
(what the app is actually talking to -- check it first, never assume).

`NOVA_API`, `CELL_NAME`, `LOG_LEVEL` come from the environment or a `.env` (the repo root has
one, gitignored). Override on the command line for a one-off, e.g.
`NOVA_API=http://<instance> LOG_DIR=/tmp/pause-logs uv run python -m audi_arg3_pause`.

## Architecture

- `app.py` -- the FastAPI app (`main()` runs uvicorn; `DEV_RELOAD=true` switches to `--reload`).
  Lifespan: start the `ControllerWatcher` and the `StatusHub`; on shutdown stop every robot
  process, then any NOVAx-started program, then the watcher. Unchanged from `../tcpswitch`.
- `controller_watcher.py` -- polls `list_robot_controllers`, registers/deregisters one
  `<controller>_pause_on_io` NOVAx program per controller. `programs.program_id()` is the one
  place the id is derived.
- `programs.py` -- the program factory and the motion. Reads the home joints once, builds
  `[joint_ptp(home + delta on joint 0), joint_ptp(home)]`, plans once (or every cycle with
  `replan`), then loops: stop IO -> `execute(trajectory, tcp, actions, pause_on_io=...)`.
  `enable_condition()` is the one place the condition is built:
  `motion_enable_signal(io)` for the fail-safe wiring, and an explicit inverted `PauseOnIO`
  with a warning when the operator asks for "move while False". A failure is logged with the
  observers' snapshot and re-raised -- **no retries around motions**.
- `observe.py` -- `SignalWatcher` (the enable IO over NATS), `TrajectoryWatcher` (the motion
  group's state on its **own** websocket) and `ExecutionObserver`, which wraps each `execute()`
  with a heartbeat and the stall detector. See "Reading a log" below.
- `observe.ExecutionObserver.run_execution` owns the motion task rather than wrapping an
  `await`, because both bounds (`fail_after_stall_s`, `MOTION_TIMEOUT_S`) have to be able to
  interrupt it. **A cancelled motion finishes as `CancelledError`, which is a `BaseException`**
  and would sail straight past the program's `except Exception` and end the run as a clean exit
  -- so the watchdog's verdict is checked before the task's, and `ExecutionAbandoned` is raised
  instead. That was a real bug, caught only because the test asserted the exit code.
- `run_program.py` -- the per-robot worker. Configures its own rotating log file first thing and
  `logger.exception`s before re-raising, because the parent never reads its output.
- `runner.py` -- one subprocess per robot, incremental start, per-robot stop, exit-code reaping.
  `_OPTION_FLAGS` maps a run option to its CLI flag; adding an option means touching that dict,
  `programs.py`'s defaults and `web_ui.RUN_OPTIONS`, and nothing else.
- `status.py` -- `StatusHub`, folds the SDK's `.programs` and `.cycle` NATS events into one
  record per controller.
- `web_ui.py` -- serves `static/` and the API. `/api/config` carries `title`, the `pause`
  variant and the seven `run_options`; `tcp_selection` stays at the default `"single"`.
- `logs.py`, `iocreate.py` -- copies of the sdk app's (log files, rotation budget, zip, clear;
  gate-IO create/delete on virtual bus-IO services only).
- `static/` -- byte-identical copy of the repo's shared `ui/`. **Never edit `static/` directly**:
  edit `ui/`, run `scripts/sync-ui.sh`, commit every copy.

### Reading a log

A run's log is written to be read top to bottom by someone who was not there. The order is
fixed: what was configured, what condition was sent to the controller, then per cycle a line
before `execute()`, the observers' transitions, a heartbeat every 2 s while it is open, and a
line when it returns. Both bracket lines carry the same snapshot, so a cycle can be judged
without reading the middle.

| line | what it settles |
| --- | --- |
| `pause condition sent to the controller: {...}` | what was actually armed, not what was meant |
| `wandelbots-nova <version>` | which SDK produced this log |
| `enable IO 'start' changed False -> True (change #N)` | when the signal moved, from NATS |
| `trajectory state X (standstill=..) -> Y at location L` | what the controller reported, transitions only |
| `in execute() 12.0s (beat #6) \| ... \| allowed to move` | the signal and the robot, side by side, while waiting |
| `STALL: allowed to move but standing still for N s` | **the reported fault** |
| `LINGER: the trajectory reached its end N s ago` | not the fault: the socket is closing |

The SDK's own decisions are in the same file: `move_forward` logs `Movement paused (IO
condition) at location L` and `Pause signal cleared — resuming movement` at INFO, so they are
there without `verbose`. `verbose` adds DEBUG for the cursor, the state machine and
`io_condition`, which is where `Paused trajectory state observed before the current operation
showed any motion` and every `StartMovementRequest` show up.

**STALL vs LINGER is the distinction to get right**, and it is the only logic in the app with
automated checks (`scripts/check_stall_detector.py`, 11 cases, no instance needed). Standing
still while enabled is normal at the end of a trajectory; it is a fault when the trajectory has
not finished. The two are told apart by how far the location travelled *in this execution*
(`TrajectoryWatcher.window_span`), not by the state alone -- because a terminal frame with zero
travel is precisely the stale-frame shape that wedged `execute()` before (see
`../sdk/docs/pr-516-field-report.md`). The plain last-seen location cannot answer it: between
two cycles it still holds the previous trajectory's end.

### Why the observer opens its own state stream

The SDK fans **one** websocket per motion group out to all its subscribers, and `execute()` is
one of them. Going through `motion_group.stream_state()` would therefore add no independent
observation at all, and would pin the shared socket to the observer's rate -- changing the
execution being observed. `OBSERVE_STATE_RATE_MS` (default 100 ms) is deliberately separate
from the run's `state_rate_ms`, which is a variable under test; `-1` switches the observer
stream off for a run that must carry no extra websocket. Same reasoning as
`../tcpswitch/scripts/tcp_switch_repro_stream_load.py`.

### The three scenarios

`manual` (default) never writes the enable signal. `enabled_once` reads and waits for it, then
commands one execution and finishes -- the test for "does a clean execution start at all",
with no pause and no resume involved. `auto_resume` drops the signal, commands the execution,
waits `enable_delay_ms` and raises it again, once per cycle: that is the pause/resume path
driven unattended, ~4.3 s per attempt on the virtual cell, which is what turns "it sometimes
wedges" into a rate. Pair it with `fail_after_stall_s` so a wedge does not park the robot.

### `MOTION_TIMEOUT_S` defaults to 0 here, unlike the siblings

`../sdk`, `../api`, `../rust` and `../tcpswitch` bound `execute()` at 300 s because a wedged
execution there is always a fault. In this app an execution that sits still can be entirely
correct: with the enable signal low the robot is *supposed* to wait, for as long as the operator
leaves it low. A timeout would also destroy the wedged state the run exists to capture. So the
detector reports and the run keeps going; set `MOTION_TIMEOUT_S` when a bound is wanted anyway.

The consequence is that **`Stop all` in the UI is the way out of a wedged robot.** The stop IO
is only polled between cycles, so a robot inside `execute()` never reaches that check.

### Motion limits

`TCP_VELOCITY_MM_S` (200), `TCP_ACCELERATION_MM_S2` (500), `TCP_JERK_MM_S3` (2500) are env
overridable, same values and same reasoning as `../tcpswitch`: TCP limits bound a joint PTP too
(the planner applies both), so a KR240's flange at ~1.5 m radius rotates at most ~8 deg/s at
200 mm/s. On a physical robot with a heavy tool keep these conservative and let the payload
resolve (the SDK picks the payload registered under the TCP's name, as `../api/CLAUDE.md`
explains at length).

### Verified 2026-09-22 against the virtual instance at 172.31.13.120

Seven `VirtualController`s (left over from the SDK team's own pause work: `kuka-pause-on-io-test`,
`kuka-bus-pause-test`, `ur-bus-pause-test`, ...), a `profinet_virtual` bus-IO service, `start`
and `stop` created through the UI's ＋ button. Exercised on `kuka-pause-on-io-test`:

- enable low at the start -> `PausedByUser` then `PausedOnIO` at location 0, `execute()` stays
  open, heartbeat says "paused by the enable signal", **no** stall reported (correct);
- enable raised -> `Pause signal cleared — resuming movement`, `Running`, cycle completes;
- 16 cycles back-to-back at ~2.6-5.3 s each;
- enable dropped mid-motion -> on-path pause at location 1.9514, resumed on the next edge;
- stop IO raised -> loop exits after the current cycle, exit code 0.

**The fault did not reproduce on this virtual cell**, which is why the detector has offline
checks. Re-verify before assuming: the instance's contents drift.

## Code style

Same as `../sdk` (from its `.github/copilot-instructions.md`): deliberately beginner-friendly
Python, plain functions, short functions, basic type hints, `logging` not `print`, never
`time.sleep()` in async code, `line-length = 100`. The swallow-and-continue `except Exception`
blocks around IO reads and NATS publishes are intentional: an unconfigured IO or a broken event
bus must not kill a run. `ruff` is capped below 0.16 so this app lints against the same rule set
as its siblings.
-- README
# audi_arg3_pause — deployed as `audi-arg3-pause`

A NOVA app (FastAPI via NOVAx, on the [NOVA Python SDK](https://github.com/wandelbotsgmbh/wandelbots-nova))
that reproduces a **robot that stays in standstill at the start of an execution although its
enable signal allows motion** — one cycle finishes normally, the next is commanded with the same
condition and the robot never starts.

Per robot the operator picks a TCP, a base-joint (joint 0) rotation from the presets
5/10/15/20/45/90 degrees (default 10) and a direction. Each cycle rotates joint 0 by that amount
and back, executed with **`pause_on_io` armed on the enable signal**: the robot is allowed to
move while that signal reads `true`, and the controller pauses it on path as soon as it reads
`false`. The SDK waits for the signal to come back and resumes, so one `execute()` covers any
number of pauses (see the SDK's `docs/architecture/adr/002-io-pause-is-resumable.md`).

## How this differs from the other apps in this repo

**Nothing waits for the signal before the motion.** The move-up apps gate the loop with
`wait_for_bus_io` on `start` and only then execute. Here the gating *is* the thing under test,
so the execution is always commanded and the controller decides whether the robot moves.

That means the shared UI's **"wait IO" field is this app's enable signal** (default `start`),
not a pre-motion gate. `stop` ends the loop as in every other app. Both are created on a virtual
bus-IO service with the ＋ button next to the fields.

Because an execution can legitimately sit still for as long as the signal is low, `execute()` is
**not** bounded by a wall-clock timeout here (`MOTION_TIMEOUT_S` defaults to `0`). A wedged robot
therefore stays wedged, on purpose — that is the state worth capturing. **`Stop all` in the UI is
the way out**: the stop IO is only polled between cycles, so a robot inside `execute()` never
sees it.

`fail_after_stall_s` is the bound that fits this app better, because it only counts time during
which the robot *was* allowed to move. Leave it at 0 while watching a single robot; set it for
an unattended `auto_resume` run.

## Run it

```bash
uv sync --locked
NOVA_API=http://<instance> uv run python -m audi_arg3_pause
open http://localhost:3000/ui
```

`GET /api/health` tells you which instance and cell the app is actually talking to. Confirm the
controllers are virtual before starting anything that moves.

One robot without the app, from a shell:

```bash
uv run python -m audi_arg3_pause.run_program ir340r01 --tcp 1 --wait-io start --stall-s 10
```

## The three scenarios

`scenario` decides how the enable signal is driven during a run. **Only `manual`
never writes it** — on a real cell it is a PLC-facing Profinet variable that the sibling apps
also use as their run-enable, so an app that writes it is gating every other ARG3 robot too.

| scenario | what it does | what it answers |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **`manual`** (default) | never touches the signal; you toggle it | anything, by hand |
| **`enabled_once`** | waits until the signal *already* allows motion, commands exactly **one** execution, finishes | does a clean execution with nothing to pause it start at all? No pause and no resume are involved, so a robot that does not move here failed from a standing start |
| **`auto_resume`** | per cycle: drop the signal, command the execution (robot held at the trajectory start), wait `enable_delay_ms`, raise it again | the pause/resume path, unattended — one resume attempt every ~4 s, so a rate instead of anecdotes |

`enabled_once` runs **one execution per process** on purpose: the question is whether the
*first* execution moves, and looping inside one process would reuse a warm SDK instead of
testing a cold one. Click *Run selected* again for another trial, and count.

`auto_resume` is the statistics engine. On the virtual cell it turns over a full
hold → execute → release → move → complete cycle every ~4.3 s, so an hour is ~800 resume
attempts. Set `fail_after_stall_s` for it (60 is sensible) so a wedge ends the cycle instead
of parking the robot until someone notices.

## Run options

| option | default | what it is for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `scenario` | manual | see above; the only option that makes the app write an IO |
| `enable_delay_ms` | 1000 | `auto_resume`: how long the robot is held before the signal is raised |
| `fail_after_stall_s` | 0 (never) | cancel an execution that has been allowed to move but standing still this long |
| `degrees` / `direction` | 10, positive | the joint-0 rotation, same presets as `../tcpswitch` |
| `state_rate_ms` | 0 (step rate) | the **execution's** state stream rate — the stream the SDK's state machine reads to decide a pause happened and a resume happened |
| `stall_s` | 10 | how long "enabled, standing still, not advancing" must hold before it is reported; 0 switches the detector off |
| `gap_ms` | 0 | idle time between cycles — separates a back-to-back race from a state that is simply wrong |
| `replan` | off | plan once and execute many (off) or plan afresh each cycle (on) |
| `verbose` | off | DEBUG for the SDK's `move_forward`, trajectory cursor, state machine and `io_condition` loggers |

Environment knobs that are not per-run: `OBSERVE_STATE_RATE_MS` (100; the observer's own stream,
`-1` disables it), `HEARTBEAT_INTERVAL_S` (2), `STALL_REPEAT_S` (30), `MOTION_TIMEOUT_S` (0),
`STATE_RESPONSE_RATE_MS` / `STALL_S` (the defaults the UI prefills), plus the usual
`NOVA_API`, `CELL_NAME`, `LOG_DIR`, `LOG_LEVEL`.

## Resume strategy (`resume`, `missed_auto_resume`)

Branch `pause-auto-resume`. Who restarts the motion after an IO pause -- not to be confused
with the `auto_resume` *scenario*, which is about the app driving the enable signal:

| `resume` | what goes on the wire | while held | who resumes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `sdk` (default) | `PauseOnIO` as before | `PAUSED_ON_IO` | the SDK sends a new start once the signal allows motion |
| `controller` | `PauseOnIO.auto_resume = true` | `RUNNING` while braking, then `WAIT_FOR_IO` | the controller, by itself (robotics/wbr!2384) |

`missed_auto_resume` only applies to `controller`: when the signal allows motion but the robot
is still held 500 ms later, `fail` (default) ends the execution ("AUTO-RESUME MISSED") so an
upstream defect stays visible, `start` sends one start from the SDK to keep the cell moving.

`controller` needs a RAE image with wbr!2384 *and* an API client that knows the field: both apps
pin `wandelbots-api-client 26.8.0+a3081.4275fd77.483450` (service-manager MR !3081) from the
internal GitLab registry (project 889, readable without credentials, `[[tool.uv.index]]`
`wandelbots-internal`). On an image without wbr!2384 the controller ignores the flag, the pause is
a terminal `PAUSED_ON_IO` again, and with `fail` the run fails at the first release -- which is
also the quickest way to find out what the image does. Roll back: check out `pause-on-io-repro`.

## Reading a log

Every run's log opens with what was configured, the **exact condition sent to the controller**
and the installed `wandelbots-nova` version — so a log always says which SDK produced it, which
matters while the pin moves along the interlock branch.

Two observers then run for the whole program and write into the same file:

- the **enable signal**, watched over NATS (the same push the SDK's own condition watcher
  reads), logging every change;
- the **motion group's own state stream**, on its own websocket, logging transitions of the
  trajectory state (`Running` / `PausedOnIO` / `PausedByUser` / `Ended`), `standstill` and the
  trajectory location.

While an `execute()` is open, a heartbeat prints both side by side every two seconds:

```
cycle 3 -- in execute() 12.0s (beat #6) | enable 'start'=True for 14.5s
         | stop 'stop'=False for 14.4s | traj=PausedOnIO standstill=True loc=0.0000 for 10.2s
         frames=138 | allowed to move
```

and the detector turns the claim into one greppable block:

```
cycle 3 -- STALL: allowed to move but standing still for 10.2s (report #1)
    enable enable 'start'=True for 14.5s, 1 change(s) this run
    traj=PausedOnIO standstill=True loc=0.0000 for 10.2s frames=138
    travelled 0.0000 in this execute() -- the execution never started
    last state frame 0.09s ago, execute() open 12.0s
    the pause condition is 'start == False'; the signal reads True, so it does NOT hold
    and the controller should be running this trajectory
```

`grep STALL` is the whole triage. A separate `LINGER` warning covers the neighbouring case —
the trajectory reached its end and `execute()` has not returned yet — so a slow websocket
teardown is never mistaken for a robot that will not start. The two are told apart by how far
the location travelled *in that execution*, not by the trajectory state alone: a terminal frame
with zero travel is a fault, not a completion.

## Minimal repro without the app

`scripts/pause_repro.py` is the same program as a single, UI-less SDK script for handing to
colleagues or to the SDK team: plain `@nova.program` + `run_program`, configured by environment
variables, with both observers and the same stall reporting inlined.

```bash
# manual: you toggle the signal
NOVA_API=http://<ipc> CONTROLLER=ir340r01 TCP=1 ENABLE_IO=start STOP_IO=stop \
  DEGREES=10 CYCLES=0 STALL_S=10 VERBOSE=true \
  uv run python scripts/pause_repro.py

# one execution with the signal already high
SCENARIO=enabled_once uv run python scripts/pause_repro.py

# unattended pause/resume, one attempt every few seconds
SCENARIO=auto_resume ENABLE_DELAY_MS=1000 uv run python scripts/pause_repro.py
```

It only needs `wandelbots-nova` installed (any environment with the SDK works), so the file can
be copied out of this repo on its own.

## Checking the detector without a cell

The fault has not reproduced on a virtual cell, so the one piece that has to be right when it
finally happens is the piece a virtual cell cannot exercise: the rule that decides STALL vs
LINGER vs silence. It has offline checks — no instance, no network:

```bash
uv run python scripts/check_stall_detector.py     # 11 cases
```

## Deploy

Exactly like `../sdk`: `skaffold dev --cleanup=false --status-check=false` for development
(hot-reloads `.py` changes into the pod), `nova app install` for the slow path. `k8s/app.yaml`
is the NOVA `App` resource; it sets neither `NOVA_API` nor `BASE_PATH` on purpose (the
app-operator injects both) and mounts a 300Mi volume at `/data` for the log files.

## The SDK pin

Unlike `../tcpswitch`, this app does **not** share `../sdk`'s pin: `pause_on_io` only exists on
the interlock branch.

```toml
"wandelbots-nova[novax,nova-rerun-bridge] @ git+https://github.com/wandelbotsgmbh/wandelbots-nova.git@lab/interlock-with-pause"
```

Locked at `e73ece8b` with `wandelbots-api-client` 26.7.0. Move it forward deliberately, run
`uv lock` and commit the lockfile — the Dockerfile copies it and `uv sync --locked` fails the
build if it drifted.

## Logs

One rotating file per robot under `LOG_DIR` (default `./logs`, `/data` in-cluster), written by
the robot's own process. The UI's Logs panel lists them, downloads single files or a zip, and
views one in the page — the last 64 KB, paging backwards on demand, with an opt-in follow that
lives only while the viewer is open. Nothing runs per log line on the writing side.

uv run ruff check --select I --fix

# CLAUDE.md

This file provides guidance to Claude Code (claude.ai/code) when working with code in this repository.

## What this is

A Wandelbots **NOVA app** (FastAPI via NOVAx, built on the NOVA Python SDK) that reproduces a
**robot that stays in standstill at the start of an execution although its enable signal allows
motion**. It deploys as **`audi-arg3-pause`**; the python package is `audi_arg3_pause`.

It is the fifth app in this repo and a close sibling of `../sdk` and `../tcpswitch` (same run
model, same operator UI, same two bus IOs). Three things differ, and all three are the point:

- **The gating happens inside the execution, not before it.** The other apps `wait_for_bus_io`
  on `start` and only then `execute()`. Here every cycle commands `execute()` immediately with
  `pause_on_io` armed on the enable signal and lets the *controller* decide whether the robot
  moves. Do not add a pre-motion wait: it would hide exactly what is being reproduced.
- **`wait_io` means the enable signal.** The shared UI's "wait IO" field is reused for it
  (default `start`), because it already carries an IO name with bus-IO suggestions and the
  create/delete buttons. `stop` ends the loop as everywhere else.
- **The enable signal can be driven by the app**, under `scenario`
  (`manual` / `enabled_once` / `auto_resume`). Only `auto_resume` writes it, and the default is
  `manual` because on a real cell that signal is PLC-facing and shared with the sibling apps.
  `enabled_once` deliberately runs **one execution per process**: the question is whether the
  *first* execution moves, so a fresh cursor, machine and websocket per trial is the point --
  do not "optimise" it into a loop.
- **`observe.py` is half the app.** The claim under test is "the signal says move and the robot
  does not", and neither half of that can be read from the SDK, since `execute()` is the
  suspect. Two independent watchers supply the evidence.

The SDK pin is **not** shared with `../sdk`: `pause_on_io` only exists on the interlock branch
(`lab/interlock-with-pause`, currently `e73ece8b`). Every run logs the installed
`wandelbots-nova` version on its first lines, so a log always says which SDK produced it.

Everything else -- one `run_program.py` process per robot, per-robot rotating log files, status
from the SDK's own NATS events, the shared UI -- is the `../sdk` design. Read `../sdk/CLAUDE.md`
for the deployment gotchas (Skaffold `resourceSelector`, `DEV_RELOAD` + `INSTALL_DEV`, never set
`NOVA_API`/`BASE_PATH` in `k8s/app.yaml`, the Dockerfile must copy `uv.lock`); they all apply
unchanged.

There is no pytest suite. `scripts/check_stall_detector.py` is the one thing that is checked
automatically, and it needs no instance.

**Branch `pause-auto-resume`** pins the SDK to `lab/pause-auto-resume` and adds the run options
`resume` (`sdk`|`controller`) and `missed_auto_resume` (`fail`|`start`).
`programs._apply_resume_strategy` sets the SDK's process-wide `ExecutionPolicy` from them at the
start of every run (one `run_program.py` process per robot keeps it per robot). See README,
"Resume strategy".

## Commands

```bash
uv sync --locked                                   # create venv + install deps
uv run python -m audi_arg3_pause                   # run the app on :3000 (blocks)
uv run python -m audi_arg3_pause.run_program <controller> --tcp 1 --wait-io start --stall-s 10
uv run python scripts/check_stall_detector.py      # offline: the stall/linger classification
uv run ruff format && uv run ruff check --select I --fix
skaffold dev --cleanup=false --status-check=false  # in-cluster dev, see ../sdk/CLAUDE.md
```

Endpoints: `/ui` (operator UI), `/api/*` (its backing API), `/programs` (NOVAx), `/api/health`
(what the app is actually talking to -- check it first, never assume).

`NOVA_API`, `CELL_NAME`, `LOG_LEVEL` come from the environment or a `.env` (the repo root has
one, gitignored). Override on the command line for a one-off, e.g.
`NOVA_API=http://<instance> LOG_DIR=/tmp/pause-logs uv run python -m audi_arg3_pause`.

## Architecture

- `app.py` -- the FastAPI app (`main()` runs uvicorn; `DEV_RELOAD=true` switches to `--reload`).
  Lifespan: start the `ControllerWatcher` and the `StatusHub`; on shutdown stop every robot
  process, then any NOVAx-started program, then the watcher. Unchanged from `../tcpswitch`.
- `controller_watcher.py` -- polls `list_robot_controllers`, registers/deregisters one
  `<controller>_pause_on_io` NOVAx program per controller. `programs.program_id()` is the one
  place the id is derived.
- `programs.py` -- the program factory and the motion. Reads the home joints once, builds
  `[joint_ptp(home + delta on joint 0), joint_ptp(home)]`, plans once (or every cycle with
  `replan`), then loops: stop IO -> `execute(trajectory, tcp, actions, pause_on_io=...)`.
  `enable_condition()` is the one place the condition is built:
  `motion_enable_signal(io)` for the fail-safe wiring, and an explicit inverted `PauseOnIO`
  with a warning when the operator asks for "move while False". A failure is logged with the
  observers' snapshot and re-raised -- **no retries around motions**.
- `observe.py` -- `SignalWatcher` (the enable IO over NATS), `TrajectoryWatcher` (the motion
  group's state on its **own** websocket) and `ExecutionObserver`, which wraps each `execute()`
  with a heartbeat and the stall detector. See "Reading a log" below.
- `observe.ExecutionObserver.run_execution` owns the motion task rather than wrapping an
  `await`, because both bounds (`fail_after_stall_s`, `MOTION_TIMEOUT_S`) have to be able to
  interrupt it. **A cancelled motion finishes as `CancelledError`, which is a `BaseException`**
  and would sail straight past the program's `except Exception` and end the run as a clean exit
  -- so the watchdog's verdict is checked before the task's, and `ExecutionAbandoned` is raised
  instead. That was a real bug, caught only because the test asserted the exit code.
- `run_program.py` -- the per-robot worker. Configures its own rotating log file first thing and
  `logger.exception`s before re-raising, because the parent never reads its output.
- `runner.py` -- one subprocess per robot, incremental start, per-robot stop, exit-code reaping.
  `_OPTION_FLAGS` maps a run option to its CLI flag; adding an option means touching that dict,
  `programs.py`'s defaults and `web_ui.RUN_OPTIONS`, and nothing else.
- `status.py` -- `StatusHub`, folds the SDK's `.programs` and `.cycle` NATS events into one
  record per controller.
- `web_ui.py` -- serves `static/` and the API. `/api/config` carries `title`, the `pause`
  variant and the seven `run_options`; `tcp_selection` stays at the default `"single"`.
- `logs.py`, `iocreate.py` -- copies of the sdk app's (log files, rotation budget, zip, clear;
  gate-IO create/delete on virtual bus-IO services only).
- `static/` -- byte-identical copy of the repo's shared `ui/`. **Never edit `static/` directly**:
  edit `ui/`, run `scripts/sync-ui.sh`, commit every copy.

### Reading a log

A run's log is written to be read top to bottom by someone who was not there. The order is
fixed: what was configured, what condition was sent to the controller, then per cycle a line
before `execute()`, the observers' transitions, a heartbeat every 2 s while it is open, and a
line when it returns. Both bracket lines carry the same snapshot, so a cycle can be judged
without reading the middle.

| line | what it settles |
| --- | --- |
| `pause condition sent to the controller: {...}` | what was actually armed, not what was meant |
| `wandelbots-nova <version>` | which SDK produced this log |
| `enable IO 'start' changed False -> True (change #N)` | when the signal moved, from NATS |
| `trajectory state X (standstill=..) -> Y at location L` | what the controller reported, transitions only |
| `in execute() 12.0s (beat #6) \| ... \| allowed to move` | the signal and the robot, side by side, while waiting |
| `STALL: allowed to move but standing still for N s` | **the reported fault** |
| `LINGER: the trajectory reached its end N s ago` | not the fault: the socket is closing |

The SDK's own decisions are in the same file: `move_forward` logs `Movement paused (IO
condition) at location L` and `Pause signal cleared — resuming movement` at INFO, so they are
there without `verbose`. `verbose` adds DEBUG for the cursor, the state machine and
`io_condition`, which is where `Paused trajectory state observed before the current operation
showed any motion` and every `StartMovementRequest` show up.

**STALL vs LINGER is the distinction to get right**, and it is the only logic in the app with
automated checks (`scripts/check_stall_detector.py`, 11 cases, no instance needed). Standing
still while enabled is normal at the end of a trajectory; it is a fault when the trajectory has
not finished. The two are told apart by how far the location travelled *in this execution*
(`TrajectoryWatcher.window_span`), not by the state alone -- because a terminal frame with zero
travel is precisely the stale-frame shape that wedged `execute()` before (see
`../sdk/docs/pr-516-field-report.md`). The plain last-seen location cannot answer it: between
two cycles it still holds the previous trajectory's end.

### Why the observer opens its own state stream

The SDK fans **one** websocket per motion group out to all its subscribers, and `execute()` is
one of them. Going through `motion_group.stream_state()` would therefore add no independent
observation at all, and would pin the shared socket to the observer's rate -- changing the
execution being observed. `OBSERVE_STATE_RATE_MS` (default 100 ms) is deliberately separate
from the run's `state_rate_ms`, which is a variable under test; `-1` switches the observer
stream off for a run that must carry no extra websocket. Same reasoning as
`../tcpswitch/scripts/tcp_switch_repro_stream_load.py`.

### The three scenarios

`manual` (default) never writes the enable signal. `enabled_once` reads and waits for it, then
commands one execution and finishes -- the test for "does a clean execution start at all",
with no pause and no resume involved. `auto_resume` drops the signal, commands the execution,
waits `enable_delay_ms` and raises it again, once per cycle: that is the pause/resume path
driven unattended, ~4.3 s per attempt on the virtual cell, which is what turns "it sometimes
wedges" into a rate. Pair it with `fail_after_stall_s` so a wedge does not park the robot.

### `MOTION_TIMEOUT_S` defaults to 0 here, unlike the siblings

`../sdk`, `../api`, `../rust` and `../tcpswitch` bound `execute()` at 300 s because a wedged
execution there is always a fault. In this app an execution that sits still can be entirely
correct: with the enable signal low the robot is *supposed* to wait, for as long as the operator
leaves it low. A timeout would also destroy the wedged state the run exists to capture. So the
detector reports and the run keeps going; set `MOTION_TIMEOUT_S` when a bound is wanted anyway.

The consequence is that **`Stop all` in the UI is the way out of a wedged robot.** The stop IO
is only polled between cycles, so a robot inside `execute()` never reaches that check.

### Motion limits

`TCP_VELOCITY_MM_S` (200), `TCP_ACCELERATION_MM_S2` (500), `TCP_JERK_MM_S3` (2500) are env
overridable, same values and same reasoning as `../tcpswitch`: TCP limits bound a joint PTP too
(the planner applies both), so a KR240's flange at ~1.5 m radius rotates at most ~8 deg/s at
200 mm/s. On a physical robot with a heavy tool keep these conservative and let the payload
resolve (the SDK picks the payload registered under the TCP's name, as `../api/CLAUDE.md`
explains at length).

### Verified 2026-09-22 against the virtual instance at 172.31.13.120

Seven `VirtualController`s (left over from the SDK team's own pause work: `kuka-pause-on-io-test`,
`kuka-bus-pause-test`, `ur-bus-pause-test`, ...), a `profinet_virtual` bus-IO service, `start`
and `stop` created through the UI's ＋ button. Exercised on `kuka-pause-on-io-test`:

- enable low at the start -> `PausedByUser` then `PausedOnIO` at location 0, `execute()` stays
  open, heartbeat says "paused by the enable signal", **no** stall reported (correct);
- enable raised -> `Pause signal cleared — resuming movement`, `Running`, cycle completes;
- 16 cycles back-to-back at ~2.6-5.3 s each;
- enable dropped mid-motion -> on-path pause at location 1.9514, resumed on the next edge;
- stop IO raised -> loop exits after the current cycle, exit code 0.

**The fault did not reproduce on this virtual cell**, which is why the detector has offline
checks. Re-verify before assuming: the instance's contents drift.

## Code style

Same as `../sdk` (from its `.github/copilot-instructions.md`): deliberately beginner-friendly
Python, plain functions, short functions, basic type hints, `logging` not `print`, never
`time.sleep()` in async code, `line-length = 100`. The swallow-and-continue `except Exception`
blocks around IO reads and NATS publishes are intentional: an unconfigured IO or a broken event
bus must not kill a run. `ruff` is capped below 0.16 so this app lints against the same rule set
as its siblings.
-- README
# audi_arg3_pause — deployed as `audi-arg3-pause`

A NOVA app (FastAPI via NOVAx, on the [NOVA Python SDK](https://github.com/wandelbotsgmbh/wandelbots-nova))
that reproduces a **robot that stays in standstill at the start of an execution although its
enable signal allows motion** — one cycle finishes normally, the next is commanded with the same
condition and the robot never starts.

Per robot the operator picks a TCP, a base-joint (joint 0) rotation from the presets
5/10/15/20/45/90 degrees (default 10) and a direction. Each cycle rotates joint 0 by that amount
and back, executed with **`pause_on_io` armed on the enable signal**: the robot is allowed to
move while that signal reads `true`, and the controller pauses it on path as soon as it reads
`false`. The SDK waits for the signal to come back and resumes, so one `execute()` covers any
number of pauses (see the SDK's `docs/architecture/adr/002-io-pause-is-resumable.md`).

## How this differs from the other apps in this repo

**Nothing waits for the signal before the motion.** The move-up apps gate the loop with
`wait_for_bus_io` on `start` and only then execute. Here the gating *is* the thing under test,
so the execution is always commanded and the controller decides whether the robot moves.

That means the shared UI's **"wait IO" field is this app's enable signal** (default `start`),
not a pre-motion gate. `stop` ends the loop as in every other app. Both are created on a virtual
bus-IO service with the ＋ button next to the fields.

Because an execution can legitimately sit still for as long as the signal is low, `execute()` is
**not** bounded by a wall-clock timeout here (`MOTION_TIMEOUT_S` defaults to `0`). A wedged robot
therefore stays wedged, on purpose — that is the state worth capturing. **`Stop all` in the UI is
the way out**: the stop IO is only polled between cycles, so a robot inside `execute()` never
sees it.

`fail_after_stall_s` is the bound that fits this app better, because it only counts time during
which the robot *was* allowed to move. Leave it at 0 while watching a single robot; set it for
an unattended `auto_resume` run.

## Run it

```bash
uv sync --locked
NOVA_API=http://<instance> uv run python -m audi_arg3_pause
open http://localhost:3000/ui
```

`GET /api/health` tells you which instance and cell the app is actually talking to. Confirm the
controllers are virtual before starting anything that moves.

One robot without the app, from a shell:

```bash
uv run python -m audi_arg3_pause.run_program ir340r01 --tcp 1 --wait-io start --stall-s 10
```

## The three scenarios

`scenario` decides how the enable signal is driven during a run. **Only `manual`
never writes it** — on a real cell it is a PLC-facing Profinet variable that the sibling apps
also use as their run-enable, so an app that writes it is gating every other ARG3 robot too.

| scenario | what it does | what it answers |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **`manual`** (default) | never touches the signal; you toggle it | anything, by hand |
| **`enabled_once`** | waits until the signal *already* allows motion, commands exactly **one** execution, finishes | does a clean execution with nothing to pause it start at all? No pause and no resume are involved, so a robot that does not move here failed from a standing start |
| **`auto_resume`** | per cycle: drop the signal, command the execution (robot held at the trajectory start), wait `enable_delay_ms`, raise it again | the pause/resume path, unattended — one resume attempt every ~4 s, so a rate instead of anecdotes |

`enabled_once` runs **one execution per process** on purpose: the question is whether the
*first* execution moves, and looping inside one process would reuse a warm SDK instead of
testing a cold one. Click *Run selected* again for another trial, and count.

`auto_resume` is the statistics engine. On the virtual cell it turns over a full
hold → execute → release → move → complete cycle every ~4.3 s, so an hour is ~800 resume
attempts. Set `fail_after_stall_s` for it (60 is sensible) so a wedge ends the cycle instead
of parking the robot until someone notices.

## Run options

| option | default | what it is for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `scenario` | manual | see above; the only option that makes the app write an IO |
| `enable_delay_ms` | 1000 | `auto_resume`: how long the robot is held before the signal is raised |
| `fail_after_stall_s` | 0 (never) | cancel an execution that has been allowed to move but standing still this long |
| `degrees` / `direction` | 10, positive | the joint-0 rotation, same presets as `../tcpswitch` |
| `state_rate_ms` | 0 (step rate) | the **execution's** state stream rate — the stream the SDK's state machine reads to decide a pause happened and a resume happened |
| `stall_s` | 10 | how long "enabled, standing still, not advancing" must hold before it is reported; 0 switches the detector off |
| `gap_ms` | 0 | idle time between cycles — separates a back-to-back race from a state that is simply wrong |
| `replan` | off | plan once and execute many (off) or plan afresh each cycle (on) |
| `verbose` | off | DEBUG for the SDK's `move_forward`, trajectory cursor, state machine and `io_condition` loggers |

Environment knobs that are not per-run: `OBSERVE_STATE_RATE_MS` (100; the observer's own stream,
`-1` disables it), `HEARTBEAT_INTERVAL_S` (2), `STALL_REPEAT_S` (30), `MOTION_TIMEOUT_S` (0),
`STATE_RESPONSE_RATE_MS` / `STALL_S` (the defaults the UI prefills), plus the usual
`NOVA_API`, `CELL_NAME`, `LOG_DIR`, `LOG_LEVEL`.

## Resume strategy (`resume`, `missed_auto_resume`)

Branch `pause-auto-resume`. Who restarts the motion after an IO pause -- not to be confused
with the `auto_resume` *scenario*, which is about the app driving the enable signal:

| `resume` | what goes on the wire | while held | who resumes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `sdk` (default) | `PauseOnIO` as before | `PAUSED_ON_IO` | the SDK sends a new start once the signal allows motion |
| `controller` | `PauseOnIO.auto_resume = true` | `RUNNING` while braking, then `WAIT_FOR_IO` | the controller, by itself (robotics/wbr!2384) |

`missed_auto_resume` only applies to `controller`: when the signal allows motion but the robot
is still held 500 ms later, `fail` (default) ends the execution ("AUTO-RESUME MISSED") so an
upstream defect stays visible, `start` sends one start from the SDK to keep the cell moving.

`controller` needs a RAE image with wbr!2384 *and* an API client that knows the field: both apps
pin `wandelbots-api-client 26.8.0+a3081.4275fd77.483450` (service-manager MR !3081) from the
internal GitLab registry (project 889, readable without credentials, `[[tool.uv.index]]`
`wandelbots-internal`). On an image without wbr!2384 the controller ignores the flag, the pause is
a terminal `PAUSED_ON_IO` again, and with `fail` the run fails at the first release -- which is
also the quickest way to find out what the image does. Roll back: check out `pause-on-io-repro`.

## Reading a log

Every run's log opens with what was configured, the **exact condition sent to the controller**
and the installed `wandelbots-nova` version — so a log always says which SDK produced it, which
matters while the pin moves along the interlock branch.

Two observers then run for the whole program and write into the same file:

- the **enable signal**, watched over NATS (the same push the SDK's own condition watcher
  reads), logging every change;
- the **motion group's own state stream**, on its own websocket, logging transitions of the
  trajectory state (`Running` / `PausedOnIO` / `PausedByUser` / `Ended`), `standstill` and the
  trajectory location.

While an `execute()` is open, a heartbeat prints both side by side every two seconds:

```
cycle 3 -- in execute() 12.0s (beat #6) | enable 'start'=True for 14.5s
         | stop 'stop'=False for 14.4s | traj=PausedOnIO standstill=True loc=0.0000 for 10.2s
         frames=138 | allowed to move
```

and the detector turns the claim into one greppable block:

```
cycle 3 -- STALL: allowed to move but standing still for 10.2s (report #1)
    enable enable 'start'=True for 14.5s, 1 change(s) this run
    traj=PausedOnIO standstill=True loc=0.0000 for 10.2s frames=138
    travelled 0.0000 in this execute() -- the execution never started
    last state frame 0.09s ago, execute() open 12.0s
    the pause condition is 'start == False'; the signal reads True, so it does NOT hold
    and the controller should be running this trajectory
```

`grep STALL` is the whole triage. A separate `LINGER` warning covers the neighbouring case —
the trajectory reached its end and `execute()` has not returned yet — so a slow websocket
teardown is never mistaken for a robot that will not start. The two are told apart by how far
the location travelled *in that execution*, not by the trajectory state alone: a terminal frame
with zero travel is a fault, not a completion.

## Minimal repro without the app

`scripts/pause_repro.py` is the same program as a single, UI-less SDK script for handing to
colleagues or to the SDK team: plain `@nova.program` + `run_program`, configured by environment
variables, with both observers and the same stall reporting inlined.

```bash
# manual: you toggle the signal
NOVA_API=http://<ipc> CONTROLLER=ir340r01 TCP=1 ENABLE_IO=start STOP_IO=stop \
  DEGREES=10 CYCLES=0 STALL_S=10 VERBOSE=true \
  uv run python scripts/pause_repro.py

# one execution with the signal already high
SCENARIO=enabled_once uv run python scripts/pause_repro.py

# unattended pause/resume, one attempt every few seconds
SCENARIO=auto_resume ENABLE_DELAY_MS=1000 uv run python scripts/pause_repro.py
```

It only needs `wandelbots-nova` installed (any environment with the SDK works), so the file can
be copied out of this repo on its own.

## Checking the detector without a cell

The fault has not reproduced on a virtual cell, so the one piece that has to be right when it
finally happens is the piece a virtual cell cannot exercise: the rule that decides STALL vs
LINGER vs silence. It has offline checks — no instance, no network:

```bash
uv run python scripts/check_stall_detector.py     # 11 cases
```

## Deploy

Exactly like `../sdk`: `skaffold dev --cleanup=false --status-check=false` for development
(hot-reloads `.py` changes into the pod), `nova app install` for the slow path. `k8s/app.yaml`
is the NOVA `App` resource; it sets neither `NOVA_API` nor `BASE_PATH` on purpose (the
app-operator injects both) and mounts a 300Mi volume at `/data` for the log files.

## The SDK pin

Unlike `../tcpswitch`, this app does **not** share `../sdk`'s pin: `pause_on_io` only exists on
the interlock branch.

```toml
"wandelbots-nova[novax,nova-rerun-bridge] @ git+https://github.com/wandelbotsgmbh/wandelbots-nova.git@lab/interlock-with-pause"

`programs._apply_resume_strategy` sets the SDK's process-wide `ExecutionPolicy` from them at the
start of every run (one `run_program.py` process per robot keeps it per robot). See README,
"Resume strategy".

## Commands

```bash
uv sync --locked                                   # create venv + install deps
uv run python -m audi_arg3_pause                   # run the app on :3000 (blocks)
uv run python -m audi_arg3_pause.run_program <controller> --tcp 1 --wait-io start --stall-s 10
uv run python scripts/check_stall_detector.py      # offline: the stall/linger classification
uv run ruff format && uv run ruff check --select I --fix
skaffold dev --cleanup=false --status-check=false  # in-cluster dev, see ../sdk/CLAUDE.md
```

Endpoints: `/ui` (operator UI), `/api/*` (its backing API), `/programs` (NOVAx), `/api/health`
(what the app is actually talking to -- check it first, never assume).

`NOVA_API`, `CELL_NAME`, `LOG_LEVEL` come from the environment or a `.env` (the repo root has
one, gitignored). Override on the command line for a one-off, e.g.
`NOVA_API=http://<instance> LOG_DIR=/tmp/pause-logs uv run python -m audi_arg3_pause`.

## Architecture

- `app.py` -- the FastAPI app (`main()` runs uvicorn; `DEV_RELOAD=true` switches to `--reload`).
  Lifespan: start the `ControllerWatcher` and the `StatusHub`; on shutdown stop every robot
  process, then any NOVAx-started program, then the watcher. Unchanged from `../tcpswitch`.
- `controller_watcher.py` -- polls `list_robot_controllers`, registers/deregisters one
  `<controller>_pause_on_io` NOVAx program per controller. `programs.program_id()` is the one
  place the id is derived.
- `programs.py` -- the program factory and the motion. Reads the home joints once, builds
  `[joint_ptp(home + delta on joint 0), joint_ptp(home)]`, plans once (or every cycle with
  `replan`), then loops: stop IO -> `execute(trajectory, tcp, actions, pause_on_io=...)`.
  `enable_condition()` is the one place the condition is built:
  `motion_enable_signal(io)` for the fail-safe wiring, and an explicit inverted `PauseOnIO`
  with a warning when the operator asks for "move while False". A failure is logged with the
  observers' snapshot and re-raised -- **no retries around motions**.
- `observe.py` -- `SignalWatcher` (the enable IO over NATS), `TrajectoryWatcher` (the motion
  group's state on its **own** websocket) and `ExecutionObserver`, which wraps each `execute()`
  with a heartbeat and the stall detector. See "Reading a log" below.
- `observe.ExecutionObserver.run_execution` owns the motion task rather than wrapping an
  `await`, because both bounds (`fail_after_stall_s`, `MOTION_TIMEOUT_S`) have to be able to
  interrupt it. **A cancelled motion finishes as `CancelledError`, which is a `BaseException`**
  and would sail straight past the program's `except Exception` and end the run as a clean exit
  -- so the watchdog's verdict is checked before the task's, and `ExecutionAbandoned` is raised
  instead. That was a real bug, caught only because the test asserted the exit code.
- `run_program.py` -- the per-robot worker. Configures its own rotating log file first thing and
  `logger.exception`s before re-raising, because the parent never reads its output.
- `runner.py` -- one subprocess per robot, incremental start, per-robot stop, exit-code reaping.
  `_OPTION_FLAGS` maps a run option to its CLI flag; adding an option means touching that dict,
  `programs.py`'s defaults and `web_ui.RUN_OPTIONS`, and nothing else.
- `status.py` -- `StatusHub`, folds the SDK's `.programs` and `.cycle` NATS events into one
  record per controller.
- `web_ui.py` -- serves `static/` and the API. `/api/config` carries `title`, the `pause`
  variant and the seven `run_options`; `tcp_selection` stays at the default `"single"`.
- `logs.py`, `iocreate.py` -- copies of the sdk app's (log files, rotation budget, zip, clear;
  gate-IO create/delete on virtual bus-IO services only).
- `static/` -- byte-identical copy of the repo's shared `ui/`. **Never edit `static/` directly**:
  edit `ui/`, run `scripts/sync-ui.sh`, commit every copy.

### Reading a log

A run's log is written to be read top to bottom by someone who was not there. The order is
fixed: what was configured, what condition was sent to the controller, then per cycle a line
before `execute()`, the observers' transitions, a heartbeat every 2 s while it is open, and a
line when it returns. Both bracket lines carry the same snapshot, so a cycle can be judged
without reading the middle.

| line | what it settles |
| --- | --- |
| `pause condition sent to the controller: {...}` | what was actually armed, not what was meant |
| `wandelbots-nova <version>` | which SDK produced this log |
| `enable IO 'start' changed False -> True (change #N)` | when the signal moved, from NATS |
| `trajectory state X (standstill=..) -> Y at location L` | what the controller reported, transitions only |
| `in execute() 12.0s (beat #6) \| ... \| allowed to move` | the signal and the robot, side by side, while waiting |
| `STALL: allowed to move but standing still for N s` | **the reported fault** |
| `LINGER: the trajectory reached its end N s ago` | not the fault: the socket is closing |

The SDK's own decisions are in the same file: `move_forward` logs `Movement paused (IO
condition) at location L` and `Pause signal cleared — resuming movement` at INFO, so they are
there without `verbose`. `verbose` adds DEBUG for the cursor, the state machine and
`io_condition`, which is where `Paused trajectory state observed before the current operation
showed any motion` and every `StartMovementRequest` show up.

**STALL vs LINGER is the distinction to get right**, and it is the only logic in the app with
automated checks (`scripts/check_stall_detector.py`, 11 cases, no instance needed). Standing
still while enabled is normal at the end of a trajectory; it is a fault when the trajectory has
not finished. The two are told apart by how far the location travelled *in this execution*
(`TrajectoryWatcher.window_span`), not by the state alone -- because a terminal frame with zero
travel is precisely the stale-frame shape that wedged `execute()` before (see
`../sdk/docs/pr-516-field-report.md`). The plain last-seen location cannot answer it: between
two cycles it still holds the previous trajectory's end.

### Why the observer opens its own state stream

The SDK fans **one** websocket per motion group out to all its subscribers, and `execute()` is
one of them. Going through `motion_group.stream_state()` would therefore add no independent
observation at all, and would pin the shared socket to the observer's rate -- changing the
execution being observed. `OBSERVE_STATE_RATE_MS` (default 100 ms) is deliberately separate
from the run's `state_rate_ms`, which is a variable under test; `-1` switches the observer
stream off for a run that must carry no extra websocket. Same reasoning as
`../tcpswitch/scripts/tcp_switch_repro_stream_load.py`.

### The three scenarios

`manual` (default) never writes the enable signal. `enabled_once` reads and waits for it, then
commands one execution and finishes -- the test for "does a clean execution start at all",
with no pause and no resume involved. `auto_resume` drops the signal, commands the execution,
waits `enable_delay_ms` and raises it again, once per cycle: that is the pause/resume path
driven unattended, ~4.3 s per attempt on the virtual cell, which is what turns "it sometimes
wedges" into a rate. Pair it with `fail_after_stall_s` so a wedge does not park the robot.

### `MOTION_TIMEOUT_S` defaults to 0 here, unlike the siblings

`../sdk`, `../api`, `../rust` and `../tcpswitch` bound `execute()` at 300 s because a wedged
execution there is always a fault. In this app an execution that sits still can be entirely
correct: with the enable signal low the robot is *supposed* to wait, for as long as the operator
leaves it low. A timeout would also destroy the wedged state the run exists to capture. So the
detector reports and the run keeps going; set `MOTION_TIMEOUT_S` when a bound is wanted anyway.

The consequence is that **`Stop all` in the UI is the way out of a wedged robot.** The stop IO
is only polled between cycles, so a robot inside `execute()` never reaches that check.

### Motion limits

`TCP_VELOCITY_MM_S` (200), `TCP_ACCELERATION_MM_S2` (500), `TCP_JERK_MM_S3` (2500) are env
overridable, same values and same reasoning as `../tcpswitch`: TCP limits bound a joint PTP too
(the planner applies both), so a KR240's flange at ~1.5 m radius rotates at most ~8 deg/s at
200 mm/s. On a physical robot with a heavy tool keep these conservative and let the payload
resolve (the SDK picks the payload registered under the TCP's name, as `../api/CLAUDE.md`
explains at length).

### Verified 2026-09-22 against the virtual instance at 172.31.13.120

Seven `VirtualController`s (left over from the SDK team's own pause work: `kuka-pause-on-io-test`,
`kuka-bus-pause-test`, `ur-bus-pause-test`, ...), a `profinet_virtual` bus-IO service, `start`
and `stop` created through the UI's ＋ button. Exercised on `kuka-pause-on-io-test`:

- enable low at the start -> `PausedByUser` then `PausedOnIO` at location 0, `execute()` stays
  open, heartbeat says "paused by the enable signal", **no** stall reported (correct);
- enable raised -> `Pause signal cleared — resuming movement`, `Running`, cycle completes;
- 16 cycles back-to-back at ~2.6-5.3 s each;
- enable dropped mid-motion -> on-path pause at location 1.9514, resumed on the next edge;
- stop IO raised -> loop exits after the current cycle, exit code 0.

**The fault did not reproduce on this virtual cell**, which is why the detector has offline
checks. Re-verify before assuming: the instance's contents drift.

## Code style

Same as `../sdk` (from its `.github/copilot-instructions.md`): deliberately beginner-friendly
Python, plain functions, short functions, basic type hints, `logging` not `print`, never
`time.sleep()` in async code, `line-length = 100`. The swallow-and-continue `except Exception`
blocks around IO reads and NATS publishes are intentional: an unconfigured IO or a broken event
bus must not kill a run. `ruff` is capped below 0.16 so this app lints against the same rule set
as its siblings.
